results.text:
I believe that the Ayatollah gave orders down to the lowest level operatives that amounted to his version of the doomsday device.  That if he were killed, then missiles should be sprayed hither and yon to all their neighbors.  Why?  Because, he thought the ensuing destruction and chaos would cause the Gulf States, and Europe, and the democrats in America, to back down and demand de-escalation and negotiation.  He thought  his benighted regime would survive because of the cowardice of his neighbors, enemies, and the United States of America.  

And the democrats echoed exactly what the old despot expected.  They bleated and moaned about how we were being dragged into a regional war that could escalate.  That it was illegal and immoral and that children were dying and...  You know the song.

What actually happened?  The Gulf States have joined the fight against Iran.  They have jets in the air and are allowing Americans to use their airspace and landing strips.  Even some of the cowards in Europe have backed down off their high horses and are -- tepidly -- supporting the operation.  

And now all the democrats have left to motivate their agreement with the -- happily deceased -- "supreme leader" is their hatred for Donald Trump.  A hatred that is so intense that, in the midst of the threat of sleeper cell terrorist attacks here in the homeland, they keep the department of homeland security defunded.  

Losers.

I'm having codex rip the ever living hell out of my empire app.  Inverting all the dependencies.  Consolidating all state changes.  Building polymorphic boundaries between components and acceptance tests.  

It's a phased approach.  Acceptance tests cannot change.  After each phase run full test suite and then manual game-play check.  

It's fast!  And every phase boundary has worked perfectly.  I'm looking forward to inspecting the code when it is done.  I think I'll have it draw me a UML diagram!

results.text:
I asked codex to apply a clean architecture solution (components and dependency inverted boundaries).  It wrote up a nice plan describing the components and the boundaries.  Then I asked it this:

› would the result of executing this plan make it easier for you to work with this system? Why?

• Yes.

Because it would reduce ambiguity and hidden side effects, which are
the main things that slow safe changes:

1. Single mutation boundary
With apply-command!, I can trace state changes in one place
instead of chasing swap! across many files.
2. Clear dependency direction
If domain/app no longer depend on atoms/UI/filesystem, changes
are localized and lower-risk.
3. More pure functions
Pure transitions are easier to reason about, test, and refactor
without breaking behavior.
4. Better failure isolation
Ports/adapters make bugs easier to classify: domain rule bug vs
UI adapter bug vs persistence bug.
5. Faster, safer edits
When invariants run after commands, regressions are caught
immediately, so iteration speed improves.

So it helps me work faster, but more importantly it makes changes
more predictable for everyone on the codebase.
